summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between statute and street is the defining feature of the Colombian context. Outright International's country overview sets strong formal protections, including ID change without medical exams, against documented killing, and the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission made the same finding from the field. A visitor should read the legal provisions as accurate but not predictive of what happens on the ground in departments where armed groups operate.

Social opinion is more divided than the statute book. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007, the Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia, and by 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress before a committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in prime-time programmes such as Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto. As of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a "se puede ser, pero no demostrar" norm. Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres, which is where visible expression is least likely to draw a response.

Discrimination carries criminal exposure: a 2011 law penalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025, the "Inconvertibles" bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro introduced 10 May 2022 having failed by 2024 and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposing the similar "Quiérele siempre" bill in 2025.
localsOnly:
Residents hold a dense set of entitlements that a short-term visitor cannot draw on. The Constitutional Court extended social security health insurance benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so same-sex couples now enjoy the main benefits heterosexual couples have on the same terms. Since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

Education and health are covered by national rulings. In 1998 the Constitutional Court held that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the coexistence manuals of all schools nationwide so that no article discriminates against children by sexual orientation or gender identity. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations to assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation, and the 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care.

A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes. The Constitutional Court has repeatedly protected public expression of same-sex affection, including the 1994 disapproval of the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple, Judgment T-268 of 2000 permitting a gay pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked, and the boardwalk and mall rulings of 2004 and 2011. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1981, the 1990s reforms equalised the age of consent at 14, and Judgment C-507 of 1999 declared unconstitutional the military prohibition on "homosexual acts".
outOfScopeNotes:
A comprehensive trans law was under consideration in the sources reviewed, and its current status is unresolved here: the inventory does not confirm whether it has been enacted, amended or stalled, nor what it would change for document markers, healthcare access or hate-crime sentencing.

Hate-crime charging in the specific cases cited is not sourced. The Millerey investigation was ordered by the president in April 2025, but no charging decision, conviction or sentence appears in the inventory, and the same is true for the Caquetá and Guajira threat campaigns. Whether the flyers and kill lists have led to arrests or protective measures is unresolved.

Kill figures come from sources with different scopes and periods and are not directly comparable: 40-plus transgender women in 2023, 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 recorded by the Attorney General's Office. The inventory does not establish a single current rate, nor whether any figure is contested by the government.

Implementation of the "trans" and "non-binary" markers on national identification documents from November 2025 is stated without detail on which documents carry them, whether regional registries apply them uniformly, or how they are treated at border control. Whether a foreign passport's gender marker affects entry decisions is not sourced. The conversion therapy bills' precise legislative stage as of the latest source is likewise unresolved.
